plate_findings.evidence: The caption identifies lumbar hyperlordosis due to sustained lumbar muscular contraction, and the in-text mention explicitly links Figure 1A to lumbar hyperlordosis.
The in-text examination description associated with Figure 1A states hypertrophy of the lumbar paravertebral muscles.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of Case 1 showing pronounced lumbar hyperlordosis and visible prominence of the lumbar paraspinal musculature, both specifically documented in the stiff-person syndrome case description. B: Clinical photograph of Case 2 in a stiff-person syndrome case series. The caption assigns lumbar hyperlordosis to this panel, and the in-text examination additionally documents right-foot plantar-arch and metatarsal deformity.

in_text_mentions: The patient reported frequent falls, dysautonomic symptoms including diaphoresis, and mood changes described as emotional lability, depressed affect, and excessive worry. On neurological examination, increased muscle tone was observed along with hypertrophy of the lumbar paravertebral muscles and hyperlordosis, associated with reduced range of motion. Gait assessment revealed a widened base of support, en bloc movement, and impaired turning (Figure 1A and Figure 2A).

On physical examination, increased muscle tone was observed, associated with reduced muscle trophism in the lower limbs, lumbar hyperlordosis, and deformity of the plantar arch and metatarsals of the right foot (Figure 1B and Figure 2B). Paraclinical studies, including thyroid profile, vitamin B12, B1, immunoassay folic acid, and creatine kinase levels (automated enzymatic method), were within normal limits. Serum testing revealed positive GAD antibodies (GAD-Abs) at 98.81 U/mL, while anti-amphiphysin antibodies were negative.
